title: Nachiketa and the First Bite
hookLine: the first bite of something good: a door, or a detour?
carry: choose the good; delight itself can be a door
tomorrow: why would a sacred book tell you to stare into an empty jar?
last: IT CAN WANDER, BUT IT CAN'T LEAVE.

cards: Phones up for the food photo, then the first real bite. A plate of something someone you love made, and for one second the taste fills everything and the to-do list goes quiet.
Some people say a quiet word of thanks before that bite; some just dig in. Either way, here is yesterday's question: a door, or a detour? This tradition doesn't hand you one answer.
Two of its old texts speak to that bite, and they pull in different directions. Let both of them talk.

teach.h: NACHIKETA SAYS NO TO DEATH'S GIFTS.
teach.b: First voice: the Katha Upanishad. A boy named Nachiketa is offered everything by Death himself: long life, wealth, chariots, music. He turns all of it down and asks his real question instead.
There are two paths, Death says: the good, shreya, and the pleasant, preya. The wise choose the good. The one who grabs chooses the pleasant.
The best case for this voice: pleasures pull, and a life led by them may never reach what lasts. Second voice: the Vijnana Bhairava.

teach.h: DWELL IN THE JOY OF EATING.
teach.b: When you're filled with the joy of eating and drinking, it says, dwell on the fullness of that joy, and great delight follows. When you see a friend after a long time apart, rest in the gladness that rises.
When the mind is absorbed in music, become one with it. The best case for this voice: the joy itself, not the plate, is a door, because nothing in the world stands outside the divine.
Now listen to what each one is careful about. The Upanishad doesn't scold joy; it warns against being led by the pleasant away from the good.
The Vijnana Bhairava doesn't say eat more; it points past the plate to the gladness, and past the gladness to the awareness it's happening in.

teach.h: ONE GUARDS THE DOOR; ONE WALKS THROUGH.
THE JOY, NOT THE PLATE, IS THE DOOR.
teach.b: The other walks through it with eyes open. Both are voices of this one tradition.

how: Hindu teachers hold both voices: the Katha Upanishad's choice of the good over the pleasant, read in many households and schools, and, in Kashmir Shaiva practice, the Vijnana Bhairava's dharanas of resting in joy.

o: a tantric book that finds a door even in a good meal
an old story about a boy who bargains with Death
a book telling seekers to give up every pleasure

games.q: two voices on delight — tap the pairs.

s: the Vijnana Bhairava tells people to indulge more
it points past the plate to the joy, and past the joy to the awareness it happens in.
in the Katha Upanishad, Nachiketa turns down Death's offer of pleasures
and Death praises him for choosing the good over the pleasant.
Hindu texts all say the same thing about pleasure
the Katha guards against the pleasant; the Vijnana Bhairava finds a door in delight.

games.q: a friend just finished a festival fast and asks if loving the feast afterward makes her 'less spiritual.' which answer lets both voices speak?
o: one text warns against being led by pleasure; another finds a door in the joy itself.
the Vijnana Bhairava says the fast was pointless, since joy is the real door.
the Katha Upanishad says enjoying the feast undoes the good of the fast.
games.why: the Katha asks who's leading, the good or the pleasant. the Vijnana Bhairava says rest in the gladness itself. neither cancels the other.

practice: If there's something to eat or drink nearby, take one small sip or bite, slowly, and let the taste fill your attention completely. Then let the taste fade and stay with the gladness that's left.
If there's nothing nearby, remember a taste you love and do the same.

wordCard.voice: The Vijnana Bhairava: a tantric book of doors, and some of them, it says, open in delight.

orig.note: Sanskrit shreya, the good, which the Katha Upanishad sets beside preya, the pleasant.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: choose the good over the pleasant, and delight itself can be a door. Day sixteen twenty-seven.

sources.ref: Vijnana Bhairava, the dharanas on the joy of eating and drinking, on meeting a friend or relative after a long time, and on absorption in music (verses 71-73 in common numbering)
Katha Upanishad 1.1.23-29 (Death offers Nachiketa long life, wealth, chariots and music; he refuses) and 1.2.1-2 (the good and the pleasant; the wise choose the good)
